_comment: WHERE EVERY VERSION PIN LIVES. One table, read by bash and by Python.
The pins are declared by the RELEASE, in the modules/*/.env files it ships
-- those are tracked, so a checkout already carries them before install.sh
runs. config.yaml's `versions:` block was a second copy of the same facts,
and the copy is what caused trouble: update_env_files re-derived .env FROM
config.yaml, so a stamped .env could be silently regressed to an older pin.
For Elasticsearch that means a node that will not open a data directory a
newer version wrote, which is not a cosmetic failure.
This file exists so the mapping itself is not duplicated in turn. Before it,
the same knowledge lived in three places: _PIN_SOURCE in lib/upgrade/plan.sh
(primary pins), the _stamp_transitive_env_from_config call sites in
lib/modules/*.sh (transitive pins), and release_module_set() in
scripts/ci/build_release_package.py (which read config.yaml instead). Three
copies of one fact is how they drift.
JSON on purpose: bash already shells out to python3 for JSON at 17 sites,
and CI's resolver is Python. A bash associative array would have had to be
parsed by Python, or duplicated into it.
primary     the pin that IS the module's version -- what an upgrade moves
and what the plan compares. Exactly one per module.
lockstep    keys that must always equal the primary. Kibana is pinned
separately but MUST equal Elasticsearch; VolWeb releases its
frontend and backend together. Listing them makes the
alignment structural instead of something to remember.
transitive  sidecar images the module runs but does not version -- its
Postgres, Redis, OpenSearch, RabbitMQ. They move on their own
schedule and are pinned independently.

volweb.note: The one module whose .env is NOT tracked -- it holds generated secrets (DJANGO_SECRET, the Postgres password) and is rendered from .env.template. Its pins therefore have to come from the template, not from a shipped .env.

standalone._comment: Pinned things that are not modules and have no module .env of their own: rule packs and data bundles. They land in the backend's .env because that is the container that consumes them.
